sanchin.name: Sanchin
sanchin.description: The foundation kata of Goju Ryu, focusing on breathing, tension, and basic movements.
sanchin.history: Passed down from Kanryo Higaonna and further developed by Chojun Miyagi.
sanchin.culturalSignificance: Represents the essence of Goju Ryu and the connection of mind, body, and breath.

step1.description: Begin in natural stance facing forward

step3.description: Perform three punches while maintaining proper breathing

step5.title: Maintain muscle tension
step5.description: Continue sequence with controlled movements and breathing

step6.title: Conclusion
step6.description: Maintain muscle tension throughout the entire form

tensho.name: Tensho
tensho.description: A flowing kata that emphasizes the soft aspects of Goju Ryu.
tensho.history: Created by Chojun Miyagi as a complement to Sanchin.
tensho.culturalSignificance: Represents the 'ju' (soft) aspect of Goju Ryu.

gekisai-dai-ichi.name: Gekisai Dai Ichi
gekisai-dai-ichi.description: The first kata in the Gekisai series, designed to introduce basic techniques and principles of Goju Ryu.
gekisai-dai-ichi.history: This kata was developed in Okinawa around 1940 by sensei Chōjun Miyagi (co-founder of Goju-Ryu) and Shoshin Nagamine. They based Gekisai Dai Ichi on Fukyugata II (a basic kata of the Itosu system, analogous to Shuri-te's Pinan) to provide young students with a simpler kata.
gekisai-dai-ichi.culturalSignificance: Gekisai Dai Ichi is a Kaishu-gata (open-hand kata) with both hard and dynamic movements. The kata contains basic movements from heavier kata, but in simplified form. The breathing is normal (no deep Naha-te breathing) and in the spirit of Goju-Ryu (hard/soft) after each tense movement, relaxation follows again.

detailedMeaning.title: Name and Meaning
detailedMeaning.content: Gekisai Dai Ichi (撃砕第一) literally means "attack and shatter" or "attack and destroy". The characters 撃 (geki) and 砕 (sai) mean "attack, strike" and "destroy, break" respectively. In combination with 大 ("dai", great) in Gekisai Dai Ichi, this becomes "great destruction" or "greatest strike". Symbolically, the name is often translated as "crush fortress" or "great destroy".

origin.title: Origin
origin.content: This kata was developed in Okinawa around 1940 by sensei Chōjun Miyagi (co-founder of Goju-Ryu) and Shoshin Nagamine. They based Gekisai Dai Ichi on Fukyugata II (a basic kata of the Itosu system, analogous to Shuri-te's Pinan) to provide young students with a simpler kata. Thus, Gekisai Dai Ichi has roots in the Okinawa-te (especially Shuri/Naha style) tradition and is strongly influenced by the more linear Shuri elements (Pinan/Fukyugata). It is not directly adopted from a Chinese kata, but rather an Okinawan creation based on existing forms (similar to Itosu's Pinan).

transmission.title: Transmission to Goju-Ryu
transmission.content: After Miyagi formulated this kata in 1940 for youth training, he passed it on to his students in the Goju-Ryu lineage. Thus, it spread within the style through Miyagi and his students (for example, Higaonna Morio, Miyazato, Yagi Meitoku). All Goju-Ryu subsystems (Jundokan, Meibukan, IOGKF, JKF Goju Kai, etc.) know Gekisai Dai Ichi as the first or second kata after basic techniques.

historicalDevelopment.title: Historical Development and Variations
historicalDevelopment.content: Originally, Gekisai Dai Ichi included, among other things, a block with the fist above the head (higher morote-tsuki) suitable for the tall American soldiers after WWII; later performances usually bring this technique to stomach or armpit height. After Miyagi's death, small variations have arisen between schools: some lineages (e.g., Meibukan) add an extra morote-tsuki at the end, while others do not. Generally, the embusen remains the same and variations are limited to angle and application of techniques.

technicalFeatures.title: Technical and Philosophical Characteristics
technicalFeatures.content: Gekisai Dai Ichi is a Kaishu-gata (open-hand kata) with both hard and dynamic movements. The kata contains basic movements from heavier kata, but in simplified form. The breathing is normal (no deep Naha-te breathing) and in the spirit of Goju-Ryu (hard/soft), after each tense movement, relaxation follows again (Kaishu style). The kata typically starts with a defensive movement, according to the principle "Karate ni sente nashi" ("in karate there is no first attack"). Stances vary (such as zenkutsu- and kiba-dachi) and emphasize both strength and relaxation, with swinging techniques (doubled kicks and punches) that emphasize the flexibility of a moving body.

controversy.title: Controversy/Variations within Goju-Ryu
controversy.content: There is little controversy; the differences between schools are subtle. Some Goju Ryu lineages (e.g., Yagi Meitoku's Meibukan versus Yamaguchi Gogen's Goju Kai) have small execution differences in Gekisai Dai Ichi (such as the height of the upper block or the rhythm of kicks), but the foundation remains consistent. In Kyokushinkarate (which Kyokushin calls a "southern kata"), there is also an own version of Gekisai Dai Ichi, because founder Mas Oyama (who went through Goju tradition) adopted this kata.

relationships.title: Relationship to other kata/Systems
relationships.content: Gekisai Dai Ichi is a direct offshoot of Itosu's Fukyugata/Pinan kata (Shuri-te). Like its partner Gekisai Dai Ni, it serves as an introduction before the deeper Naha-te kata such as Sanchin. It is essentially the harder brother of Gekisai Dai Ni. In the teaching chain, it comes before Saifa and Sanchin. Kyokushin contains it as an early kata, Shito-Ryu also has two (Higa and Miyagi versions).

modernPractice.title: Use in Modern Practice
modernPractice.content: Gekisai Dai Ichi is traditionally taught as the first or second kata for beginning students. It is intended to practice basic movements and rhythm. In competition kata (events), it rarely occurs because it is quite simple, but it is shown at demonstrations and in dojo lesson plans as a foundation. It serves primarily as a bridge to the heavier kata (such as Sanchin and Tensho) and for conditioning and basic defense training.

step1.title: Upward block (jodan uke)
step1.description:
Gekisai dai ichi was created in 1940 by Chojun Miyagi (see introduction). Gekisai dai ichi means "attack and destroy one". The kata contains various punches, blocks, strikes and kicks, performed at different heights. It is important in the execution that attention goes to the correct execution of each technique individually. Most techniques in this kata must be performed with speed and power, only the middle block (chudan uke) with muchimi. Gekisai dai ichi teaches you, among other things, to aim at vital points, gives you a good and powerful kime, and trains the alternation between tension and relaxation.

Step forward with the right foot from musubi dachi, pivot on the balls of both feet, and perform the block simultaneously. The length of your stance should be two feet. The blocking arm moves close to the body, initially horizontally across the diaphragm, then straight up, turning only at the last moment. Keep your shoulders as relaxed as possible. The arm is focused a fist-width from the forehead. The hikite arm initially goes up, stays high during the body turn, and is then actively and forcefully pulled to the side. Focus powerfully. When you block, your weight is distributed evenly over both feet. Advanced practitioners can slightly turn the elbow downwards during kime and perform the technique with a somewhat rounder motion.

step2.title: High punch (jodan zuki)
step2.description: Push off by pressing the front foot into the ground and step straight into han zenkutsu dachi (three feet long). The pelvis does not rotate with the punch. During the kime of the punch, about 70% of your weight is on the front leg. The punch is at eye level. Also use a powerful hikite and clench your teeth during kime. Primarily use the power of the push-off and movement, keeping your shoulders relaxed for as long as possible.

step3.title: Low sweeping block (gedan barai)
step3.description: Step back with your right leg into shiko dachi, simultaneously opening your pelvis and letting it drop. Keep looking to the side. The hikite is pulled back forcefully (pull your elbow back and down). Until kime, there is no tension in the arm, and the fist ends a fist-width from the knee (in bunkai, the low block is performed as an attack to the elbow and ends further from the knee). During kime, the pelvis remains open, but the tanden closes. Note: In shiko dachi, the crown of the head is up and the chin slightly tucked. The back forms an "S", the shoulder blades are together and pointing downwards. The pelvis is open and thus tilted forward, the shin is perpendicular to the floor, and the knees are directly above the feet (initially, many karateka need to actively push their knees and thighs back for this). The hip is slightly higher than the knees (water would slowly flow down the thigh). The feet (especially the big toe and the inside of the foot) are pressed forcefully into the ground and grip the floor during kime.

step4.title: Middle block (chudan uke)
step4.description: Pull the left foot towards the other foot and then in a circle forward (ankles pass each other) into sanchin dachi. The fist of the blocking hand starts far below the elbow of the other arm. The technique is performed with muchimi. This movement is executed with a fairly large circular motion, and the foot and arm move simultaneously.

step5.title: Front kick (mae geri), elbow strike and stamp (hiji ate and fumikomi geri), backfist strike (uraken uchi), low block (gedan barai) and middle reverse punch (chudan gyaku zuki)
step5.description:
The techniques in this series (except for the elbow strike and stomp) must be performed separately and forcefully. It is important to relax (in between) after each technique. In the classical execution of Gekisai Dai Ichi, there is a count stop before the backfist strike, allowing the body to relax better. The rhythm is 1-2 and 1-2-3.

Maintain the block and hikite during the front kick. The kick – lift the knee high until the thigh is parallel to the floor - is keage (i.e., without pelvic tilt and hip rotation). The kick is straight forward with the ball of the foot towards the groin. Before the kick, sink slightly onto your standing leg, and during the kick, the body is fully supported by the standing leg. You may slightly tuck your pelvis (not necessary) and do not lock it. After the kick, relax, actively pull the lower leg back until it is below the knee. From there, it is stomped down into zenkutsu dachi.

The elbow strike goes mainly forward, the fist ending at the jaw. Pull the hikite back forcefully. The elbow strike and stomp are performed together and, depending on the karateka's level, can be done in three ways:
1. The foot is stomped down, and the rebound from the ground is used in the elbow strike. The rhythm is 1 ….. 2.
2. The foot is stomped down, and immediately after, the elbow strike is performed. The rhythm in pam-bam.
3. The stomp and elbow strike are performed simultaneously. From hara, the power goes simultaneously to the foot and the elbow. This is called "splitting power".

The backfist strike is initiated from the pelvis, and during the impulse, the shoulders, elbow, and wrist remain relaxed. The technique is a whiplash (so there is no kime) to jinchu (vital point at the center of the upper lip). After the technique, the fist snaps back, and the elbow makes a 90-degree angle.

The low sweeping block makes a relatively small swing and rotates around the elbow. During execution, there is no tension in the shoulders and elbow. During focus, the arm turns slightly. The hikite is powerful.

The reverse punch is executed with a lot of power and speed. The movement begins by straightening the rear leg. This causes the pelvis to rotate in; this is used for the powerful impulse of the punch, focused and executed towards suigetsu. Also use a powerful and fast hikite.

Note: In zenkutsu dachi, the crown is up, the chin slightly in, the back straight and the feet press into the ground. The knee of the front foot is above the foot, if you look over your knee you just don't see the toes. The stance is about four feet long. The feet are more or less at the height of the sides of the pelvis; you stand in two lines.

step6.title: Foot sweep (ashi barai) and palm strike (shotei uchi)
step6.description: Pull the rear foot towards the other and make a small foot sweep; the sweeping foot maintains contact with the ground and does not pass the other. Focus on the side of the inside of the foot. Stomp the foot down in hachiji dachi (= 'natural stance') and use the rebound from the ground for the impulse to the palm strike; also use a powerful hikite (remains a fist). During the sweep, also pull your shoulder blades apart and slightly forward (the back remains straight, you keep looking forward) and also use the snapping back of the shoulder blades in the technique. In the palm strike, the shoulders and elbows are free of tension. The technique is fast and is briefly focused at eye level ("heavy strike"). In the palm strike, the fingers are straight, and the bent thumb rests against the side of the base of the index finger. Also focus on the contact point with the hypothenar (pinky heel).

step7.title: Double punch (awase zuki); middle and reverse punch (chudan and ura zuki)
step7.description:
The double punch is a small and closed form of tora guchi. Step from hachiji dachi in a straight line back (slightly diagonally) into zenkutsu dachi and actively pull your hand (as if dragging someone) to your side (knuckles remain up). Straighten your leg and put your whole body behind the double punch; use primarily the power from the ground and your back muscles (the fist of the reverse punch is above the knee).

Step forward with your left leg and do not rise during the foot switch (feet are briefly side by side; there is a moment similar to sitting on the toilet). During the foot switch, perform a middle inward block (chudan uchi uke) with the right hand and a middle outward block (chudan soto uke) with the left hand, looking (thus) at the back of both fists. Step back and simultaneously pull the fists forcefully back to the side. Use the rebound from the ground, the straightening of the leg/pelvic rotation, and the back muscles for another powerful double punch (awase zuki: ura zuki (reverse punch) and chudan zuki (middle punch)). For the fist that will make the middle punch, the hikite is at the side with knuckles up during the switch. The ura zuki (knuckles down during the switch) is to the seventh rib (denko), the chudan zuki to the 5th intercostal space, just below the nipple (ganka).

Note: Beginners may also perform the chudan soto uke as a 'regular' chudan uke, where you look at the finger side of the fist.

step8.title: Conclusion
step8.description: Open the left hand and place the right fist in the left with a small circular motion. Turn the left foot outwards, join with the right foot in musubi dachi, and simultaneously turn the hands. Close the kata.

gekisai-dai-ni.name: Gekisai Dai Ni
gekisai-dai-ni.description: The second kata in the Gekisai series, introducing more advanced techniques including open hand techniques.
gekisai-dai-ni.history: Created by Chojun Miyagi as progression from Gekisai Dai Ichi.
gekisai-dai-ni.culturalSignificance: Builds upon the foundation established in Gekisai Dai Ichi.

detailedMeaning.title: Name and Meaning
detailedMeaning.content: Gekisai Dai Ni (撃砕第二) shares the characters 撃砕 with Dai Ichi: "attack and destroy". The suffix 小 (sho) in the Japanese name (sometimes Gekisai Sho) means "small" or "least", in contrast to 大 (dai) = "large". Freely translated, Gekisai Dai Ni means "small attack and destruction". Like Dai Ichi, the name emphasizes the idea of powerful striking, but as a counterpart to the "large" Gekisai.

origin.title: Origin
origin.content: Gekisai Dai Ni, like Dai Ichi, originated in 1940 in Okinawa under the leadership of Chōjun Miyagi (together with Shoshin Nagamine). It is based on Itosu's Fukyugata Ichi (again an analog of Pinan). Essentially, Miyagi took Fukyugata Ichi as the basis for Gekisai Dai Ni, creating two new kata to supplement the Goju curriculum. This kata again reflects the fusion of Okinawa-te with South Chinese elements, but is primarily a modern Okinawan design.

transmission.title: Transmission to Goju-Ryu
transmission.content: Like Gekisai Dai Ichi, this kata was passed on by Miyagi to his students within Goju-Ryu. It was introduced as the second Gekisai kata alongside Dai Ichi, so that young students received a more complete basic program. Important Goju founders (such as Higaonna Morio, Miyazato, Yagi Meitoku) introduced this kata at their establishments, spreading it throughout all Goju-Ryu lines.

historicalDevelopment.title: Historical Development and Variations
historicalDevelopment.content: Gekisai Dai Ni has also remained relatively unchanged. After the war, many dojos switched to blunt fists instead of the original high punch, just like with Dai Ichi. Some schools have small execution differences (stance, transition techniques). In Kyokushin, Gekisai Dai Ni is not directly adopted from Goju (although there is a so-called southern kata "Gekisai" in Kyokushin), but in Goju itself the kata remains quite consistent between Meibukan, Jundokan and Koepka-ha.

technicalFeatures.title: Technical and Philosophical Features
technicalFeatures.content: Gekisai Dai Ni, like Dai Ichi, is a Kaishu-gata. Here too, powerful strikes alternate with relaxed back-and-forth movements, fitting the Goju philosophy of hard-soft. For example, there is a deep forward punch and both high and low blocks. Breathing is flat (Kaishu) and there is relaxation on each technique. The kata contains elements of more complex kata, but simplified. According to modern students, it develops movement coordination and strength and stimulates the principle "relax after each attack".

controversy.title: Controversy/Variations within Goju-Ryu
controversy.content: There are no major disputes around Gekisai Dai Ni; the differences between schools are marginal. Most variations lie in details (such as the execution of morote-zuki). In general, this kata is practiced equally in all Goju-Ryu styles and seen as a simple exercise form.

relationships.title: Relationship to other kata/Systems
relationships.content: Gekisai Dai Ni forms the introduction of the Goju-ryu kata arsenal together with Dai Ichi, preceding Saifa and Sanchin. It is connected to Itosu's Fukyugata Ichi and the North/East Okinawa traditions (Shuri/Pinan). It emphasizes movement succession in multiple directions (similar to Pinan). Outside Goju, the name is not used much, although the intention is the same as Gekisai Dai Ichi.

modernPractice.title: Use in Modern Practice
modernPractice.content: Gekisai Dai Ni is usually taught as the second kata, after Dai Ichi. It serves primarily educational purposes (technique and rhythm). In competitions it rarely occurs (too low advanced), but at demonstrations it shows the basic principles of Goju-Ryu. It is also used as a warm-up or form of fitness training due to the fluid, fast transitions.

step1.title: Middle-high pulling block (chudan hiki uke)
step1.description:
Gekisai dai ni means "attack and destroy 2" and the kata was also developed by Chojun Miyagi, in the same period and for the same reason as Gekisai dai ichi. Gekisai dai ni is very similar to Gekisai dai ichi, only more open hand techniques appear in the second part of the kata. The differences from Gekisai dai ichi are: (1) if the kata is performed classically on count, the front kick, elbow strike, backfist strike, low sweeping block and reverse punch are on one count (the rhythm is 1 – 2 (elbow and stamp) – 3 – 4 – 5); (2) the second middle-high block is an open hand pulling block (hiki uke); (3) right and left pulling blocks (hiki uke) are added and (4) the final technique is not a powerful, double punch in a linear zenkutsu dachi, but a tora guchi with muchimi, in nekoashi dachi, stepping out of the line of attack. Besides the focus points you learn from Gekisai dai ichi, this kata teaches you the execution of blocks with open hand and the shifting focus at various blocks. Only the techniques that differ from Gekisai dai ichi are treated.

The movement is performed with muchimi, the foot moves in a circular motion (ankle along ankle), simultaneously with the hand. The blocking hand starts angled under the elbow of the other. The power is focused on the little finger side of the hand during the block. This is a circular movement; only at the end of the block is the hand pulled linearly about 5 centimeters toward the body from the elbow; the elbow then comes against the ribcage. Focus on the thumb and index finger when pulling. The hikite is also an open hand with fingers up.

step2.title: Right – left pulling block (migi hidari hiki uke)
step2.description: These two pulling blocks are admittedly performed quickly, but still separately and with muchimi. They are similar to the first pulling block, only faster. Here too the ankle goes along the ankle, simultaneously with the hand movements which also start angled under the elbow. The right foot is placed on the ground, briefly carries about 50% of the body weight and, after the block is fully executed, pushes off for the same circular movement back. During the kick the block is maintained and the hand - unlike Gekisai dai ichi and the first one in ni - is therefore open. It is pulled back just as hard for the elbow strike, turns in the process and becomes a fist.

step3.title: Tora guchi "Tiger Mouth"
step3.description:
High controlling block with the back of the hand (jodan haishu osae uke), an inward hook block (uchi kake uke) and a high and low push (jodan and gedan oshi).

From hachiji dachi (natural stance) you step in a straight line diagonally backward and pull the other foot straight in nekoashi dachi. The movement is performed with muchimi. Breathe in during the blocks, breathe out during the push. Focus on the tanden, the large back muscles and the side of the hands during the blocks; during the push focus on the tanden, the large back muscles, the palms and the thumb. During the blocks the focus point shifts: for the high block from the little finger side of the arm to the top of the wrist; for the low technique from the side of your wrist to the palm. During the push the palm is open and the thumb is joined. The tanden remains closed during the push, but the pelvis remains in the natural stance. The upper hand ends at collarbone/throat height, the lower at height of your thigh.

During the movement the entire sole of both feet remains on the ground. Therefore place your front foot completely on the ground before the movement. Note that the hand that will make the high block starts angled under the elbow of the other arm.

step4.title: Closing and remarks
step4.description:
Before closing, turn as a whole from the tanden toward the front; the feet do not come off the floor.

Note. In neko ashi dachi the crown is up, the chin slightly in and the back straight. Your weight rests mainly on the back foot (90%); from your front foot the toes and ball lightly touch the floor, as if floating. The heel of the back foot and the ball of the front foot are along a straight imaginary line (or from musubi dachi the front foot goes straight forward). The knee of the front foot falls slightly inward.

Bring the left hand up and then move both hands in a circular motion downward and place the right hand in the left, palms up. Push off powerfully with the ball of the front foot as you step back from neko ashi dachi into musubi dachi. You turn your hands and close the kata.

saifa.name: Saifa
saifa.description: An advanced kata that emphasizes powerful closed-fist techniques and aggressive impact movements.
saifa.history: Saifa was introduced to Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned the kata from Ryu Ryu Ko. The original creator of the kata is unknown, but they undoubtedly had ties to Crane Boxing. Goju-ryu is the only karate style that has Saifa in its curriculum. Saifa means something like 'destructive attacks,' but the name is more commonly used, for example, for completely different quans in Shaolin Kung Fu.
saifa.culturalSignificance: The kata is characterized by, among other things, the high number of striking techniques, which are naturally circular and executed without tension in the wrist, elbow, and shoulder. There is also only minimal use of the upper body muscles, so that the student learns to optimally use the impulse from the legs and pelvis during the stroke.

step1.title: Hazushi waza (release technique)
step1.description:
Saifa was introduced to Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned the kata from Ryu Ryu Ko. The original creator of the kata is unknown, but they undoubtedly had ties to Crane Boxing. Goju-ryu is the only karate style that has Saifa in its curriculum. Saifa means something like 'destructive attacks,' but the name is more commonly used, for example, for completely different quans in Shaolin Kung Fu. The kata is characterized by, among other things, the high number of striking techniques, which are naturally circular and executed without tension in the wrist, elbow, and shoulder. There is also only minimal use of the upper body muscles, so that the student learns to optimally use the impulse from the legs and pelvis during the stroke. As a result, this kata involves a lot of alternation between tension and relaxation.

From musubi dachi you first sink, after which you push off powerfully from the back leg, moving the front leg 45 degrees diagonally forward. The movement is smooth and is sometimes compared to a swimming octopus. You only rise once the feet are together; during the movement, keep the back straight and the crown of the head up.

step2.title: Jodan uraken uchi and osae uke
step2.description: The rhythm of the movement from the starting position to the hazushi waza, the hazushi waza itself, and the uraken uchi/osae uke is smooth/flowing – powerful – fast.

step3.title: Sukui uke, shotei gedan harai uke, hiza ate and mae geri
step3.description: Unlike the previous movements in shiko dachi (straight line), this movement is circular; the foot first goes towards the other foot and the ankles pass close to each other. Then the foot moves parallel to shomen.

step4.title: Morote zuki and morote gedan uchi
step4.description: After the (second) kick, you turn your head forward, move the leg powerfully backward into a zenkutsu dachi, and simultaneously perform the morote zuki.

step5.title: Chudan hiki uke and morote zuki
step5.description: The hand for the hiki uke starts angled under the upper arm. You do not step aside, but you swing the foot aside.

step6.title: Ashi barai, tettsui uchi, tsukami hiki and ura zuki
step6.description: The ashi barai is small, the foot goes past the other foot, and you stomp it into hachiji dachi.

step7.title: Gyaku zuki
step7.description: Turn from hachiji dachi to han zenkutsu dachi; three feet long. The punch is at throat level, above the collarbone.

step8.title: Haito uchi
step8.description: Take a long sliding step towards the rear, open the hands, and turn into a neko ashi dachi.

step9.title: Tora guchi
step9.description: Perform the tora guchi in a similar way as in Gekisai dai ni and close the kata.

seiyunchin.name: Seiyunchin
seiyunchin.description: Seiyunchin was introduced in Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned the kata from Ryu Ryu Ko. The original creator of the kata is unknown. Seiyunchin means “control and push”. This corresponds to unbalancing (or pulling) someone, controlling and attacking with a short-distance technique (attack to a vital point, throw, joint lock). Seiyunchin is the kata in which you develop a lot of “chiru no chan chan” - push-off power or explosive power. The kata has a large number of movements over a considerable distance, both forwards and backwards. Additionally, the kata contains a large number of techniques performed in shiko dachi (see the gedan barai in Gekisai dai ichi for points of attention). During a movement from shiko dachi to shiko dachi, the body remains low and the feet slide across the floor. In the kata, shiko dachi occurs several times, but each time the way the movement takes place and how the power is delivered is different.
seiyunchin.history: Seiyunchin was introduced in Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned the kata from Ryu Ryu Ko. The original creator of the kata is unknown.
seiyunchin.culturalSignificance: Seiyunchin means “control and push”. This corresponds to unbalancing (or pulling) someone, controlling and attacking with a short-distance technique. Seiyunchin is the kata in which you develop a lot of “chiru no chan chan” - push-off power or explosive power.

step1.title: Morote sukui uke and morote gedan barai
step1.description:
Seiyunchin was introduced in Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned the kata from Ryu Ryu Ko. The original creator of the kata is unknown. Seiyunchin means “control and push”. This corresponds to unbalancing (or pulling) someone, controlling and attacking with a short-distance technique (attack to a vital point, throw, joint lock). Seiyunchin is the kata in which you develop a lot of “chiru no chan chan” - push-off power or explosive power. The kata has a large number of movements over a considerable distance, both forwards and backwards. Additionally, the kata contains a large number of techniques performed in shiko dachi (see the gedan barai in Gekisai dai ichi for points of attention). During a movement from shiko dachi to shiko dachi, the body remains low and the feet slide across the floor. In the kata, shiko dachi occurs several times, but each time the way the movement takes place and how the power is delivered is different.

The entire movement is executed with muchimi. From musubi dachi, step diagonally forward in a straight line into shiko dachi. The hands go up slightly simultaneously, turn and then go sideways; they circle around the lower abdomen as if around the belly of a heavily pregnant woman. Keep the shoulder low and the fingers together, the thumb pressed against the side of the index finger.

step2.title: Sukui uke, hiki uke and nukite zuki
step2.description: This movement is also slow and with muchimi. Open both hands. The hikite goes to the side of the body, hand open and palm up. In the sukui uke, the direction of focus changes from inward-sideways, to diagonally upward and upward. The hiki uke is small and executed from the wrist.

step3.title: Hojo oshi and suri ashi
step3.description: For the hojo oshi, place the fist in your open hand and together they rotate until the thumb pad of the supporting hand is behind the thumb pad of the fist hand. From shiko dachi, pull the front leg backward into a “high nekoashi dachi” (but it is not a stance, but one continuous movement). The suri ashi ('sliding step') is fast and powerful, the feet slide across the floor.

step4.title: Ushiro and chudan hiji ate
step4.description: After the push, turn the fist tateken (vertical), the open hand turns with it and stays behind the thumb pad on the fist. This open hand stays “stuck” so that the fist is “pulled loose” for a powerful uraken hiji ate (backward elbow strike), while you simultaneously step backward into han zenkutsu dachi.

step5.title: Hojo uke
step5.description: The technique is executed with muchimi. The fist hand goes past seigetsu and begins on the left side next to your body, where it comes to rest in the palm of the other hand and together they follow the path of a chudan uke (middle-level block). Press the thumb of the open hand firmly and extend this hand.

step6.title: Ippon gedan barai
step6.description: From renoji dachi, step with the back leg diagonally forward, the ankles go closely past each other. The gedan barai is executed with much power and speed. During the technique, the pelvis opens and falls into the shiko dachi and this is used in the first gedan barai. Keep the arm more or less straight.

step7.title: Shotei chudan uke and hari uke
step7.description: From shiko dachi, pull the front foot back and move to a shiko dachi perpendicular to the front of the hall. The foot makes an arc and goes past the other foot, the pelvis remains open, the back straight, the feet slide over the floor and you don't come up. The chudan uke (middle-level block) goes with the turning of the body.

step8.title: Jodan uchi uke and uraken uchi
step8.description: From shiko dachi, turn on the left leg and make a swinging step from outside to inside (comparable to a large foot sweep, imagine sweeping someone under the ankle). Move from hara and come forward with the whole body. Both arms also make a large movement and come from outside to inside.

step9.title: Chudan yoko uke and gedan barai
step9.description: Step sideways with the front foot into a kind of bensoku dachi (scissor stance). Sink (approx. 10 cm) with your full weight deep into the front foot (imagine screwing this foot into the ground). Then push off powerfully with this foot (imagine the screw bouncing back powerfully from the ground) and use this power for the 135-degree turn.

step10.title: Age zuki, jodan uraken uchi and gedan barai
step10.description: Push off from your back leg and keep your right hand in ‘ura zuki’. Your left hand is open and above your forehead. At the moment your foot comes down, pull your left hand powerfully and actively to your solar plexus and execute a powerful age zuki. Kiai!

step11.title: Hazushi waza/Hiji ate
step11.description: For a good execution of the hazushi waza, you must imagine that you are being attacked from behind (as in the bunkai). Concentrate on the back of your body. The arm of the front leg lies against the body and goes to execute the release technique; it lies under the arm that shoots back for the uraken hiji age (backward elbow strike).

step12.title: Shotei otoshi uke and jodan uraken uchi
step12.description: From neko ashi dachi, move from the tanden with the whole body a considerable step with suri ashi forward into sanchin dachi and simultaneously execute (as two circles) a shotei otoshi uke and jodan uraken uchi.

step13.title: Morote kuri uke
step13.description: For the kuri uke, the hands make a fairly large circle upward and come together above the forehead, the backs of the little finger pads against each other, after which the elbows also come together. Bring them slowly downward, with muchimi. Focus in the elbows as they go down.

shisochin.name: Shisochin
shisochin.description: Shisochin means 'four openings' or 'four directions'. The kata is characterized by many powerful open hand techniques and attacks in four directions.
shisochin.history: Shisochin was introduced to Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned the kata from Ryu Ryu Ko. The original creator of the kata is unknown. Goju-ryu is the only karate style that practices this kata.
shisochin.culturalSignificance: The kata uses many powerful open hand techniques. An open hand arm can be relaxed more easily than a fist, allowing for faster technique execution. It also emphasizes fighting in four directions.

sanseru.name: Sanseru
sanseru.description: Sanseru means '36': 6 (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind) x 6 (color, voice, smell, taste, touch and justice). It combines Dog Kung Fu techniques with typical Goju-Ryu elements, featuring close range combat like throws and joint locks.
sanseru.history: Sanseru was introduced to Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned it from Ryu Ryu Ko. Originally creator unknown, likely from 'Dog Boxing' (Dog Kung Fu). Goju-ryu is the only karate style with this kata.
sanseru.culturalSignificance: The kata is characterized by many close-range techniques such as joint locks and ground fighting. '36' refers to the 6 senses times 6 consciousness elements.

sepai.name: Sepai
sepai.description: Sepai literally means 18 (hands), 6 (color, voice, taste, smell, touch and justice) x 3 (good, bad and peace). The kata is characteristic of Goju-Ryu due to the contrasts between hard and soft, fast and slow. Hikite occurs less frequently and most movements are two-handed techniques.
sepai.history: Sepai was introduced to Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned the kata from Ryu Ryu Ko.
sepai.culturalSignificance: Represents the 18 (6x3) elements of consciousness and action.

kururunfa.name: Kururunfa
kururunfa.meaning: Holding on Long and Striking Suddenly
kururunfa.description:
This kata is a very quick kata. It is characterised by very fast movements of the hands (mostly open-hand techniques), feet and hips. For this reason, and because of its perfectly balanced combination of go and Ju techniques, it is a very important kata in Goju Ryu. The very essence of Goju Ryu is displayed in perfect harmony within Kururunfa.
Sabaki is a key feature in this kata. There are three main kinds: moving to the side, zigzag Sabaki and twisting of the hips. All are performed with great speed and agility. Low stances such as neka ashi dachi and long zen kutsu dachi are emphasized when moving.
This kata contains certain unique and distinctive features.
For example, gyaku nage waza which uses the shoulder as a focus point when performing an arm joint attack, and an angled age zuki, performed simultaneously with a block (rising at 45° from the horizontal rather than 90°).
kururunfa.history: One of the original kata from China, specific style unknown.
kururunfa.culturalSignificance: Emphasizes the principle of 'Muchimi' and controlling the opponent.

sesan.name: Sesan
sesan.description:
This kata was handed down to Higaonna Kanryo Sensei by Ryu Ryuko Sensei in China. It was the favorite kata of Miyagi Chojun Sensei and his top student, Shinzato Jinan; therefore it was the kata which they performed most often. Miyagi An’ichi Sensei has said that when Miyagi Chojun Sensei performed this kata his eyes would sparkle; his toes gripped the floor firmly to create a stance so powerful that he seemed to be rooted to the ground, and his punch was unbelievably fast and powerful. The outstanding feature of this kata is the combination of circular and straight movement, speed with heavy powerful muchimi, and hard and soft technique. The circular smoothness of the blocks and the linear power of the attacks combine to create a kata of sublime aesthetic beauty.
Sesan kata, like Kururunfa, contains a great variety of contrasting techniques. For example circular movements quickly change to linear movements in combination; fast and slow movements are performed with muchimi and a minimum of excess body motion. This kata is characterized by combinations of techniques containing fast explosive movements balanced and interspersed by slower heavy movements performed with muchimi. Each technique, seeming to be only one strike or block, may contain many meanings. For example, towards the end of the kata a mae geri is performed. It appears to be only one movement, but in fact, a combination of three techniques is involved. Other unusual techniques are sun zuki (short punch) and snake-like movements which help you stick to your opponent in close combat fighting.
sesan.history: One of the original kata from China, likely from Monk Fist Boxing or Lion's Fist.

suparinpei.name: Suparinpei
suparinpei.description: Suparinpei is the most advanced kata of Goju-Ryu. It contains the largest number of techniques and variations. The name 'Suparinpei' and the kanji used for it mean '108'. The number 108 has a special meaning in Buddhism, representing the 108 earthly desires.
suparinpei.history: Based on the Chinese form Peichurin. Suparinpei was adapted into Goju-Ryu and represents the culmination of the system's principles.
suparinpei.culturalSignificance: The number 108 is calculated from 36 x 3. The 36 represents the calculate of spirits of the Heavens and 72 Earthly spirits. In Buddhism, it is believed possible to conquer the 108 passions/earthly desires.
